pos: n. (a town of Moab named in the ballad of the Amorite conquest of Heshbon)
etymology: Hebrew Nophach, a blast, or a breathing out, from naphach, to blow or breathe; named once, Numbers 21:30.
biblical_def: Nophah occurs in a fragment of ancient poetry Moses set into his narrative: “We have shot at them; Heshbon is perished even unto Dibon, and we have laid them waste even unto Nophah, which reacheth unto Medeba” (Numbers 21:30). The song is a taunt — the Amorites' own ballad celebrating their conquest of Moab under Sihon — and Moses quotes it to explain how the land Israel had just taken from Sihon had ceased to be Moabite before Israel arrived. The preceding verse is part of the same poem: “Woe to thee, Moab! thou art undone, O people of Chemosh: he hath given his sons that escaped, and his daughters, into captivity unto Sihon king of the Amorites” (Numbers 21:29). Israel had been forbidden to touch Moab. By quoting the Amorite song, Scripture establishes that the territory Israel took had been Amorite spoil for a generation, which is precisely the argument Jephthah would make to the Ammonites three centuries later. Nophah is named once, in a borrowed verse, to settle a question of title.

corruption_summary: Israel's conquests are cited as indiscriminate land-seizure; Numbers 21 quotes a pagan war-song to prove the ground had changed hands before Israel came near it.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel was explicitly forbidden to take Moab's land or Ammon's or Edom's. What Israel took east of Jordan was Sihon's, and Sihon had taken it from Moab in a previous war. Moses makes the point by quoting the Amorites' own boasting: “For Heshbon was the city of Sihon the king of the Amorites, who had fought against the former king of Moab, and taken all his land out of his hand” (Numbers 21:26).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's wars have boundaries, stated in advance and documented afterward. The nations Israel was told to leave alone were left alone; the one that attacked Israel on the road was destroyed. A town named in an enemy's ballad is part of the record of title.

pos: n. (one of the places in Judah to which David sent of the spoil of Ziklag)
etymology: Hebrew Siphmoth, fruitful places, or bare places, of uncertain root; named once, 1 Samuel 30:28.
biblical_def: Siphmoth is one of the towns on David's list of gifts: “And to them which were in Aroer, and to them which were in Siphmoth, and to them which were in Eshtemoa” (1 Samuel 30:28). David had just recovered everything the Amalekites took from Ziklag, with a great quantity of plunder besides, and he did an unexpected thing with it: “And when David came to Ziklag, he sent of the spoil unto the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the LORD” (1 Samuel 30:26). Thirteen places are then named, ending “to them which were in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt” (1 Samuel 30:31). He was a fugitive without a throne, and he distributed his spoil to the towns of Judah that had sheltered him. Within days Saul was dead and the men of Judah came to Hebron to anoint him king. Siphmoth was one of the towns that received the present.

corruption_summary: Generosity before power is read as political calculation; David gave away the spoil of Ziklag when he had no prospect of a crown and no claim on anyone.
corruption_paragraphs: It is easy to read 1 Samuel 30:26-31 as electioneering, and the outcome at Hebron a few weeks later encourages it. But the gift was made by a man whose city had just been burnt, whose wives had just been carried off, and whose own men had spoken of stoning him. He had no kingdom and no guarantee of one. He gave the spoil away and called it the spoil of the enemies of the LORD, which is a statement about whose victory it was.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that what God gives is given to be distributed, and that the open hand before the honour is the measure of the man. Thirteen towns are named, including places nobody can now find, because the generosity was particular and someone kept the list.

pos: n. (the plain of the soothsayers, a landmark near Shechem)
etymology: Hebrew Me'onenim, observers of times, enchanters, or soothsayers, the plural participle of anan, to practise soothsaying; named once, Judges 9:37.
biblical_def: Meonenim is a place named for a sin. In the Hebrew it is not a proper name at all but a common noun: the plain, or oak, of the soothsayers. It appears as Gaal watches Abimelech's ambush descend on Shechem: “And Gaal spake again and said, See there come people down by the middle of the land, and another company come along by the plain of Meonenim” (Judges 9:37). The margin at that verse renders it the regarders of times. The same participle stands in the law's catalogue of forbidden practices: “There shall not be found among you any one that maketh his son or his daughter to pass through the fire, or that useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch” (Deuteronomy 18:10). A landmark outside Shechem took its name from the diviners who worked there — a standing monument, in the middle of Israel, to a thing God had forbidden on pain of death.

Deuteronomy 18 puts observing times in the same sentence as making a son pass through the fire, and gives the reason: “For these nations, which thou shalt possess, hearkened unto observers of times, and unto diviners: but as for thee, the LORD thy God hath not suffered thee so to do” (Deuteronomy 18:14).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God has given His people prophecy and finally His Son, and has forbidden every other way of seeking the future. The verse that follows the prohibition is the promise of the Prophet like unto Moses. A plain outside Shechem was named for the men who took the forbidden road, and it was still called that in the days of the judges.

pos: n. (a mount of the east, the limit of the dwelling of the sons of Joktan)
etymology: Hebrew Sephar, a numbering, or a scroll, from saphar, to count or to write; named once, Genesis 10:30.
biblical_def: Sephar marks the far edge of the table of nations: “And their dwelling was from Mesha, as thou goest unto Sephar a mount of the east” (Genesis 10:30). The sons of Joktan — thirteen of them, of the line of Shem through Eber — occupied the country between those two points, which is to say the southern part of the Arabian peninsula. The verse is one of several in Genesis 10 that fix a people within actual boundaries rather than leaving them as names. Neither Mesha nor Sephar can now be located with certainty. What the chapter accomplishes does not depend on our locating them: it accounts for the whole of mankind, from Japheth's isles of the Gentiles in the north to Joktan's mount of the east, as the descendants of three brothers off one ark. Sephar's name comes from the root for counting and for writing a book, which is a fitting name for a boundary at the end of a list.

corruption_paragraphs: Several of the places in Genesis 10 are unidentifiable today, and the inference is sometimes drawn that the chapter is imaginative geography. The inference does not follow. The writer gave boundaries his readers could use; four thousand years have lost the referents. Every ancient document has this property, and it tells us nothing about whether the document is true.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is confidence in Scripture's claims where our own information has run out. The chapter's own summary is its point: “These are the families of the sons of Noah, after their generations, in their nations: and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood” (Genesis 10:32).

pos: n. (the king of Egypt whom the LORD promised to give into the hand of his enemies)
etymology: Hebrew Par'oh Chophra, from the Egyptian royal title Pharaoh with the king's own name; the Authorized Version writes the two as one word; named once, Jeremiah 44:30.
biblical_def: Pharaohhophra is named once, and only to be given up: “Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will give Pharaohhophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, and that sought his life” (Jeremiah 44:30). The setting is the last recorded scene of Jeremiah's ministry. The remnant of Judah had fled to Egypt against his word, taking him with them, and in Egypt they had resumed burning incense to the queen of heaven and told the prophet to his face that they would not hear him. This was the sign given that God's word against them would stand: “And this shall be a sign unto you, saith the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, that ye may know that my words shall surely stand against you for evil” (Jeremiah 44:29). The great power they had fled to for safety would itself be handed over, exactly as Zedekiah had been.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no refuge stands against the word of God, and that the strength men flee to is itself held in His hand. The sign He gave was not a wonder in the sky but the fall of a Pharaoh, which duly came.

pos: n. (the father of Elhanan the Bethlehemite, who slew the brother of Goliath)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'arey Oregim, forests of weavers; the Authorized Version prints it as one name; named once, 2 Samuel 21:19, where the parallel at 1 Chronicles 20:5 gives the father's name as Jair.
biblical_def: Jaareoregim is named once, as a father: “And there was again a battle in Gob with the Philistines, where Elhanan the son of Jaareoregim, a Bethlehemite, slew the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the staff of whose spear was like a weaver's beam” (2 Samuel 21:19). The parallel in Chronicles names the father Jair and names the giant: Elhanan slew Lahmi the brother of Goliath. The second element of the Hebrew here, oregim, is the word for weavers, and it appears again at the end of the same verse in the phrase a weaver's beam, which is how the Authorized Version's own margin at 1 Chronicles 20:5 notes the matter. The chapter is a short roll of four Philistine giants killed by David's men — Ishbibenob by Abishai, Saph by Sibbechai, this one by Elhanan, and the man of great stature with six fingers and six toes by Jonathan the son of Shimea. The house of the giant that had defied Israel was cut down man by man.

corruption_summary: Differences between parallel accounts are presented as contradictions; the Authorized Version's own margins record the variants and let the reader see them.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Samuel 21:19 and 1 Chronicles 20:5 differ in two particulars: the father's name, and whether the man slain was Goliath's brother or Goliath. Chronicles is the fuller and plainer reading, naming Lahmi the brother of Goliath, and the Authorized Version follows it in supplying the brother of in Samuel. The translators recorded the variant in the margin rather than concealing it, which is the honest way to hand a reader a hard place.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is confidence in the providentially preserved text together with candour about its difficulties. “These four were born to the giant in Gath, and fell by the hand of David, and by the hand of his servants” (2 Samuel 21:22). The substance of the chapter is not in doubt, and a dictionary that hid the variant would be less trustworthy, not more.

pos: n. (a son of Jahdai; also a son of Caleb by Maachah, father of Madmannah)
etymology: Hebrew Sha'aph, division, or friendship, of uncertain root; named twice, 1 Chronicles 2:47 and 2:49.
biblical_def: Two men of this name stand within three verses of each other in the Calebite genealogy. The first: “And the sons of Jahdai; Regem, and Jotham, and Geshan, and Pelet, and Ephah, and Shaaph” (1 Chronicles 2:47). The second: “She bare also Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah, and the father of Gibea: and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah” (1 Chronicles 2:49). The second Shaaph is a son of Caleb by his concubine Maachah, and he is called the father of Madmannah, a town in the south of Judah toward Edom. The idiom of father here means founder: a man's name attaches to the settlement his household raised, as Salma is called the father of Bethlehem. Achsah, named in the same verse, is Caleb's daughter who asked her father for springs of water with her field in the south. The chapter is the slow record of how one clan became a region.

corruption_paragraphs: Chronicles calls a man the father of a town, and a modern reader takes it for loose speech. It is exact speech within its own idiom: the household multiplied, settled a site, and the site bore the name of the man whose sons built it. Madmannah appears in Joshua's list of the cities of Judah toward the coast of Edom, a real place with a real register behind it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God builds His people through families, and that towns, tribes and nations are households enlarged. The same chapter that names Shaaph names Achsah, who asked her father for the upper and the nether springs, because land without water is no inheritance.

pos: n. (a son of Shobal in Judah; also the head of a family of the Nethinims; written Reaia of a Reubenite)
etymology: Hebrew Re'ayah, the LORD hath seen, from ra'ah, to see, with Yah; named at 1 Chronicles 4:2 and Ezra 2:47, and as Reaia at 1 Chronicles 5:5.
biblical_def: The name belongs to three men. The first is of Judah: “And Reaiah the son of Shobal begat Jahath; and Jahath begat Ahumai, and Lahad. These are the families of the Zorathites” (1 Chronicles 4:2). The second heads a Nethinim household in the roll of the return: “The children of Giddel, the children of Gahar, the children of Reaiah” (Ezra 2:47). The third is a Reubenite, whose name the Authorized Version spells Reaia: “Micah his son, Reaia his son, Baal his son” (1 Chronicles 5:5). The meaning is a confession that God sees — the same claim Hagar made in the wilderness when she called the LORD Thou God seest me, and the same root in the name of the place she named. Three unconnected families in three different tribes gave a son this name over several centuries, which says something about how ordinary the confession was in Israel.

corruption_summary: Being seen is now a social good to be sought and granted; the Hebrew name says that God sees, which is comfort and warning at once.
corruption_paragraphs: To be seen has become a thing people ask of one another, and failing to see someone is counted a wrong. The biblical confession is different in object and in effect. It is not that others see me but that God does — which comforted a runaway slave girl in the desert and terrified a king on his roof. “And she called the name of the LORD that spake unto her, Thou God seest me” (Genesis 16:13).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the omniscience of God as a settled fact of daily life, not a doctrine kept in a cupboard. Three families in three tribes named sons for it. The Nethinim household that bore the name came back from Babylon to cut wood for the temple, unseen by everyone except the One the name confesses.

pos: n. (a son of Shobal the Horite, a duke of Seir; written Shepho in Genesis)
etymology: Hebrew Shephi, bareness, or a bare high place, from a root signifying to be smooth or bare; named once in this spelling, 1 Chronicles 1:40.
biblical_def: Shephi belongs to the Horite genealogy, the people who held mount Seir before Esau's descendants dispossessed them: “The sons of Shobal; Alian, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. And the sons of Zibeon; Aiah, and Anah” (1 Chronicles 1:40). Genesis gives the same list with slightly different spellings: “And the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam” (Genesis 36:23). His grandfather is identified in the verse that heads the list: “These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who inhabited the land; Lotan, and Shobal, and Zibeon, and Anah” (Genesis 36:20). What is notable is that Scripture preserves the genealogy of a people who were neither Israelite nor, strictly, Edomite — the Horites were the land's prior inhabitants, and Moses set down their fathers' houses as carefully as Israel's own. The name means a bare height, the kind of treeless ridge that country is made of.

corruption_summary: Scripture is assumed to record only the covenant people; Moses set down the fathers' houses of the Horites, a nation Israel never fought and God had already displaced.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 36 gives two long genealogies: Esau's and the Horites'. Neither is Israel. The Horites were dispossessed before Israel ever came that way: “The Horims also dwelt in Seir beforetime; but the children of Esau succeeded them, when they had destroyed them from before them, and dwelt in their stead” (Deuteronomy 2:12). The chapter preserves their dukes and their sons anyway.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the God of Scripture is the God of all the earth and keeps account of nations that never knew Him. A son of a Horite duke is named in the Bible, under two spellings, in two books, because the record is of the world and not merely of the church.

pos: n. (the third son of Rehoboam by Abihail the daughter of Eliab)
etymology: Hebrew Zaham, loathing, or fatness, of uncertain root; named once, 2 Chronicles 11:19.
biblical_def: Zaham is one of three sons born to Rehoboam by his first wife: “Which bare him children; Jeush, and Shamariah, and Zaham” (2 Chronicles 11:19). The marriage is described a verse earlier: “And Rehoboam took him Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David to wife, and Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse” (2 Chronicles 11:18). What follows is the account of a house dividing: “And after her he took Maachah the daughter of Absalom; which bare him Abijah, and Attai, and Ziza, and Shelomith” (2 Chronicles 11:20), and then the plain statement, “And Rehoboam loved Maachah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines: (for he took eighteen wives, and threescore concubines; and begat twenty and eight sons, and threescore daughters.)” (2 Chronicles 11:21). The crown went to Maachah's son Abijah because his father loved his mother best. Zaham is a son of the unfavoured wife in a polygamous house, which is the oldest unhappiness in the Bible.

corruption_summary: Polygamy is defended from the lives of the patriarchs and kings; Scripture narrates it and narrates, every time, the ruin it produced in the house.
corruption_paragraphs: That godly men in Scripture took more than one wife is used as an argument that the practice is permissible. The record itself argues the other way. Every polygamous house in the Bible is a house at war: Sarah and Hagar, Leah and Rachel, Hannah and Peninnah, David's sons murdering one another, and here Rehoboam's eighteen wives, sixty concubines, and a succession settled by preference rather than by birthright. The law from the beginning was one man and one woman: “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's narration is not its approval. Rehoboam “made Abijah the son of Maachah the chief, to be ruler among his brethren: for he thought to make him king” (2 Chronicles 11:22), and three sons of another wife were passed over. The Holy Ghost recorded their names anyway.
